The dwarf gourami, Trichogaster lalius, is a labyrinth fish from Pakistan, northern India and Bangladesh. All the fish in the trade are mass-produced, and several line-bred colour forms are sold, including 'Sunset' and 'Neon'. Stock quality has fallen badly, and mass-breeding may have spread dwarf gourami iridovirus (DGIV), which appears to be very infectious and can pass to other species sharing the water.

  • Max size: 88 mm SL (3.5 in)
  • Temperature: 22–27°C (72–81°F)
  • pH: 6.0–7.5
  • Hardness: 2–18 dGH
  • Difficulty: 5 of 8 (easy)

• Family: Belontiidae
  • Origin: India (West Bengal, Assam) and Bangladesh
  • Social: Peaceful
  • Tank level: Top and mid-dweller
  • Minimum tank size: 5 gallons (about 19 litres)
  • Diet: Omnivore, will eat algae
  • Breeding: Egglayer, bubble nest
  • Care: Intermediate
  • Adult size: 2 inches (about 5 cm)
  • Life expectancy: 4–6 years
  • pH: 6.0 to 7.5
  • Hardness: 4 to 10 dGH
  • Temperature: 22 to 28 °C (72 to 82 °F)

• Scientific name: Trichogaster lalius (formerly Colisa lalia)
  • Water type: freshwater
  • Minimum tank size: 15 gallons (~60 litres)
  • Breeding: easy to medium
  • Dwellers: top to mid-dwelling
  • Nitrate: less than 60
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 2 years
  • Colour form: predominantly scarlet with slanted stripes (natural colour)

Trichogaster lalius was once a popular aquarium fish known for its sparkling colour and resistance to poor water quality, but it has lost its hardiness over the past decade due to extensive selective breeding, Asian disease and poor maintenance in mass production. It is no longer recommended for beginners. Besides being less hardy, it is also very timid and stressed easily.

Wild Trichogaster species are hardy and highly adaptive, but the same cannot be said for selectively bred Dwarf Gouramis. With these variants it is somewhat of a gamble, and unless the right conditions are provided, problems are not uncommon. Buying juveniles is recommended, as younger gouramis adapt more readily to a new environment. Do not introduce them during or immediately after aquarium cycling; wait at least a couple of weeks until the balance is fully established.

Problems associated with Dwarf Gouramis:

  • Diminished quality: the high popularity of this species has harmed its overall quality. Mass production facilities have for many years used various additives and stimulants to increase profit, resulting in a significant decline in quality.
  • Dwarf Gourami Iridovirus (DGIV): there is a widespread epidemic of DGIV, a highly infectious Megalocytivirus that has proven untreatable. Research in Australia in 2006 found that a considerable percentage of dwarf gouramis from the Asian market carried this disease.
  • Overbreeding and inbreeding: inbreeding is intentionally practised to create genetic uniformity for a specific colour or pattern, but it weakens the immune system and makes the fish more prone to disease.
  • Health issues: because of compromised immune systems and stress, keeping this species often leads to health problems, which can frequently prove fatal.

Some pet shops have stopped stocking them due to difficulties in obtaining healthy, disease-free stock. Finding a local breeder may be a safer option.

Widely distributed through Pakistan, northern India and Bangladesh. Apparent occurences in Nepal and Myanmar are now thought to be as a result of misidentification. Feral populations also exist in a handful of countries, including Singapore, the USA and Colombia. Nowadays all the fish on sale in the trade are mass-produced for the purpose and you're very unlikely to encounter wild caught specimens on sale.

Originating in India (West Bengal and Assam) and Bangladesh, the dwarf gourami is native to thickly vegetated waters. It is often found together with other gourami species in the genus Trichogaster (also known as Colisa). In the river plains of northern India, larger gourami species are among the most common food fish and are sold dried or as fish-meal in many markets.

Trichogaster lalius is native to Asia. It is widely distributed in Nepal (Koshi, Narayani and Karnali rivers), India (West Bengal), Pakistan, Myanmar and Bangladesh.

In recent years it has also become established, through intentional releases and accidental escapes, in Australia, Colombia and the United States.
Predominantly inhabits sluggish, heavily-vegetated environments including ponds, swamps, ditches, streams and irrigation canals.

In the wild these fish are mostly found in stagnant fresh water such as pools, ditches, ponds, wetlands, rice fields, irrigation channels, lakes and marshes. Sometimes they are also found in slow-flowing streams and rivers.

Dwarf gouramis prefer shallow areas or other quiet habitats where they can hide in leaf litter and dense aquatic vegetation.

According to some studies they can reach 8.8 cm in length, but in aquariums the average adult size is about 5–7 cm total length. The body is egg-shaped and strongly compressed laterally. The mouth is small and directed upwards. The dorsal and anal fins are soft-rayed; the tail fin is rounded to truncate. The pelvic fins are long, thread-like feelers that can be moved in all directions. The body is predominantly scarlet with slanted pale blue stripes running downwards and backwards from the back to the abdomen. There can also be scarlet spots and bars on the fins and a red margin on the anal fin. The lateral line is incomplete.

Selective breeding has produced many colour morphs, including “Blue”, “Neon blue”, “Red”, “Super red”, “Fire red”, “Blue diamond”, “Cobalt”, “Rainbow” and “Multicolored”.

These fish have an accessory respiratory organ, the labyrinth organ, located beside the gill cavities. It consists of folded membranes supported by a bony framework, densely packed with blood vessels and functioning much like lungs, which lets the fish breathe air at the surface and survive where oxygen levels in the water are low.
A 24" x 12" x 12" (60cm x 30cm x 30cm) - 56 litre tank is just about big enough for a pair provided it is set up correctly (see section below).

This small fish suits small to medium-sized tanks.

  • A single Dwarf Gourami: a 10-gallon (40-litre) tank is enough.
  • A small group of 2–3 (for example 2 females and 1 male): around 20–30 gallons (80–120 litres) is a good starting point.

A larger tank is better: they are territorial and can be quite aggressive with each other if there is not enough space; water balance and parameters are easier to maintain in larger volumes; and conditions are more stable, diluting potential fluctuations in water chemistry. Long tanks are better than tall tanks of the same volume.

Plenty of hiding spots and ample vegetation help reduce stress and aggression, but this is hard to achieve in small tanks.

Like most Anabantoids, dwarf gouramis do not appreciate fast-moving or turbulent water. Try to keep flow to a minimum in any set-up containing them. They do best in a heavily-planted tank with plenty of shade and hiding places. The addition of a dark substrate and floating vegetation is also recommended to calm these essentially shy fish. The addition of some twigs, branches and leaf litter could make for a very natural-looking set-up. That said, the modern tank-bred fish are fairly adaptable and can thrive in most well-maintained aquaria, provided they have sufficient hiding places and shady areas. These are important to provide refuges for the female in the face of male harassment, also in a sparsely decorated tank the species becomes shy and withdrawn much more easily.

Dwarf gouramis are well suited to smaller aquariums as well as community aquariums. Gouramis can be skittish when subjected to noise and should be kept in a quiet location. Provide plenty of vegetation, including floating plants that cover only part of the surface of the water, as these labyrinth fish need access to the surface of the aquarium to breathe air.

Lifespan: there is no data on the maximum lifespan in the wild. Many guides suggest up to 5 years, but in the vast majority of cases they live a maximum of 2 years even with appropriate care. Factors that strongly influence lifespan:

  • Temperature: high temperatures (above 25°C) accelerate metabolism and reduce lifespan by nearly half.
  • Frequent mating: continuous breeding leads to physical exhaustion and shortens life.
  • Genetics: stress and weak genetics, often associated with selective breeding, have significantly affected longevity.

Fish bought from stores are typically already 4 to 6 months old, which should be considered when estimating lifespan.

Tankmates: suitable tankmates are small fish that are not big enough to eat or harass them, such as mollies, neon tetras, cardinal tetras, Endler's livebearers, pygmy corydoras, guppies, zebra danios, harlequin rasboras, clown killifish, least killifish and otocinclus.

Dwarf gouramis should not be kept with dwarf shrimp. They are predators and will eat anything that fits in their mouths, including shrimplets, and even adult shrimp after moulting may be eaten. Heavy planting gives some protection, but in the long run it is a bad idea. Opinions on snails vary: they are often seen to ignore snails, at most nipping at their antennae, though some reports describe gouramis eating snails.

Avoid large, aggressive or boisterous fish (cichlids, large barbs, goldfish, etc.) and long-finned fish (angelfish, bettas, etc.). Keep them away from crayfish and most freshwater crabs.

• Temperature: 22–27°C (72–81°F)
  • pH: Wild fish tend to inhabit environments containing soft, acidic water. The tank-bred fish are more adaptable and can normally be maintained anywhere within the range 6.0 - 7.5.
  • Hardness: 2–18 dGH

Temperature: 20–26°C. They can tolerate slightly cooler water if acclimated very slowly. In a 90-day experiment at 20, 25, 30 and 35°C, the optimal temperature for growth and weight gain was 25°C. Survival was higher at 20°C and 25°C (only 1% mortality), whereas at 28°C mortality was already 10%. The temperature lethal to 50% of the population was 39°C. Temperatures outside the optimal range significantly affect growth and development.

pH: in a study, the best growth, survival and culture conditions were seen at pH 7.0. The lethal concentration (50% mortality) was at pH 5.71 and 8.22. Below pH 6.5 or above 7.3, the fish risk skin problems and infections that can be hard to treat, and become more susceptible to oodiniosis (velvet disease). The recommended aquarium range is pH 6.5–7.5.

Hardness: medium to slightly hard water; anything in the range of 4–12 GH is acceptable.

Salinity: poorly tolerated. Experiments showed they can be safely exposed to up to 4 g/L without mortality, while 5.81 g/L was the maximum lethal salinity.

Nitrate: less than 60.

Lighting: subdued lighting is best. In planted tanks, lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants. According to a study, a 16-hour light period gave the highest absolute, specific and relative growth rates compared with 0L:24D and 12L:12D, attributed to photostimulation and increased feed intake that improve feed conversion efficiency.

Flow: these fish prefer stagnant water in the wild, so avoid strong water currents, which can stress them.

Substrate: it does not play a significant role and could even be skipped. However, in a bare-bottom tank, light reflecting off the bottom can confuse the fish and make them nervous, so at least a thin layer of substrate is better.

Filtration: any filter suited to the size of the tank is fine.

Decorations: provide lots of hiding places, as they are skittish. Provide many floating plants, where they like to rest. Dense, tall plants such as Vallisneria, Ludwigia, Elodea and Anacharis divide territory and help a female tired of the persistent advances of males.

Thought to be omnivorous in nature, feeding on small invertebrates, algae and other aufwuchs. It accepts most foods offered in the aquarium, and a good quality dried food is acceptable as the staple diet. Supplement this with regular meals of small live and frozen foods such as bloodworm for the fish to develop the best health and colouration.

In nature, gouramis eat small insects and larvae from the surface of the water and graze on algal growth on rocks and plants. In captivity, they will eat flake food, freeze-dried food, frozen foods, and vegetable tablets. To maintain good health, supplement their diet with periodic feedings of live foods such as worms. Live foods should also be used to condition breeder pairs.

Trichogaster lalius is omnivorous with a predominantly carnivorous appetite. They are not picky and will eat both animal and plant matter (algae). In the wild they feed on detritus, debris, micro-zooplankton, worms, insects and small crustaceans.

In aquariums they enjoy a wide variety of live foods, including brine shrimp, daphnia, bloodworms, tubifex worms, blackworms, grindal worms and cyclops. For best growth and colour, feeds should contain about 30–40% protein, 4–9% lipids and 30–40% carbohydrates. According to a study, 35% protein gave the greatest increase in weight and length; in general gouramis require 30–45% protein, 4–9% lipids and 30–40% carbohydrates.

They can also be reared on dry and freeze-dried foods such as flakes, pellets and crisps, as long as they suit the mouth size.

Colour enhancement: they cannot synthesise carotenoids and must obtain them from food. Astaxanthin and canthaxanthin are common carotenoid supplements that enhance colour, particularly red and orange hues. Foods containing astaxanthin, spirulina and krill (natural sources of astaxanthin) can improve colour over time.

Feeding: scientifically, daily food equivalent to about 3–5% of body weight is needed. In practice the “5-minute rule” works well: the fish should eat all the food within 5 minutes, and leftovers are a sign of overfeeding. Since they are not fast swimmers, food should be spread over a wider area if faster fish share the tank.

Fry: after yolk sac absorption, fry require live food (rotifers, vinegar eels, microworms or infusoria) for the next 2–3 weeks, then Artemia from the 3rd week. In one experiment, fry fed live food had a 100% survival rate, egg yolk 66%, and commercial pellets only 46%. Daphnia and cyclops are not recommended for fry: they can be too big, and large cyclops may harm or kill small fry. Hydras are among the worst enemies and can destroy a whole brood in a short time.

The dwarf gourami comes with a reserved recommendation for the community tank, not least because of associated health issues (see notes below). It can certainly be kept alongside numerous other species, but is not exactly the "ideal" community fish. It's both shy and territorial, so in a small tank should be considered the primary inhabitant. The addition of other anabantoids (including Bettas) or gaudy species such as guppies can cause some male dwarf gouramis to become very aggressive, whilst housing them with larger or more vigorous tankmates can have the opposite effect. Non-threatening shoals of small, peaceful cyprinids such as the Harlequin Trigonostigma heteromorpha, many rasboras and some barbs therefore make excellent companions in the more modest set-up. Loaches including Yasuhikotakia sidthimunki or any of the various Pangio species are also good choices. Some of the currently popular freshwater shrimps such as the cherry shrimp Neocaridina denticulata can also work well in a planted tank. If geography is not an issue, many of the commonly available tetras, catfish (Corydoras and Otocinclus are particularly suitable) and smaller rainbowfish could also be added. In larger set-ups any territorial behaviour is naturally less obvious and other gouramis or even some peaceful cichlids can be considered. Tankmates should still be chosen with care though, and should not be too large, active or aggressive to intimidate the dwarves or outcompete them for food.

It's generally not a good idea to keep a group of dwarf gouramis together and the species is usually sold in sexed pairs. We've noticed an alarming tendency towards tanks containing solely males in the trade during recent years, and must stress that buying two males is a recipe for disaster unless you have a very large tank. Buying a male and female pair is by far the best way to keep this species. Even then problems can arise as males can be very hard on females on occasion.

The dwarf gourami is a peaceful and shy fish. When kept in pairs, they tend to swim together. This species is usually peaceful and can be kept with other species that are not too large or aggressive. Other brightly colored species can sometimes cause male gouramis to become aggressive as they are mistaken for rivals. Peaceful, small schooling fish are suitable tankmates, as are most bottom-dwelling fish. Potential tankmates include dwarf cichlids, cardinal tetras, or neon tetras.

Temperament: most articles describe Dwarf gouramis as peaceful and gentle, suitable for community aquariums. They are very shy and hide from loud sounds and even slight disturbances. This is generally true in large, heavily planted tanks, but with caveats:

  • Despite their small size, males become very territorial during breeding and will fight, chase and nip other fish in the tank.
  • Males kept together often fight, and one may be killed if there is not enough space for each to claim a territory.
  • Mixing males and females is not without risk: males can become excessively aggressive when trying to breed, harming or even killing females.

Sociality: the species feels more confident in a group (3–4), but this can lead to conflicts, especially in the breeding season. Keeping a single fish is advisable, especially in a small tank with limited vegetation. When alone, their peaceful nature emerges.

Activity: they are relatively active swimmers, though not frantic. They examine anything new in the tank with their feelers. They can jump out of the tank, though it is uncommon and usually happens when stressed or when water quality is poor.

Placement: they prefer the middle and top layers of the tank.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: average
  • Peaceful: yes (conditionally)
  • Nippers: yes
  • Jumpers: yes (rarely)

Males are a little larger and much more colourful than the plainer, silvery females. They also develop extended dorsal and anal fins as they mature which the females lack. There are several colour morphs available, but all can be sexed very easily using this method.

Males are generally larger than females and more vividly colored. As males reach maturity, they develop elongated dorsal and anal fin tips that come to a point. In females, these fins are shorter and rounded.

Only mature fish show sexual dimorphism:

CharacterMaleFemale
Body sizeLargerSlightly smaller
Body colourBrightly colouredLess colourful (silvery or dull silvery)
Colour patternOblique lateral bands on the body are peacock blueBands are dull steel grey
Upper lipMore pronouncedLess pronounced
Fin morphologyDorsal and pelvic fins more pointed at the posterior end; dorsal fin longer, reaching the middle of the caudal peduncleDorsal and pelvic fins rounded or curved
Fin colourPelvic fin a single ray that later becomes orange-red; in breeding season dorsal and anal fins become peacock blue with an orange borderPelvic fin yellowish-grey; in breeding season dorsal and anal fins become yellowish-grey
Abdomen (breeding season)Slender bellyBulging abdomen
Bubble nestBuilds bubble nestsNo
TemperTerritorial and more aggressivePeaceful

Like many anabantoids, it's a bubble-nesting species. Breeding is not too difficult, although the males can be somewhat unpredictable in terms of behaviour. You'll need to set up a separate tank for spawning purposes. Something around 18"-24" in length is fine. There's no need to use a substrate, but a handful or two of peat fibre may be beneficial. Also add some good sized clumps of hornwort or other fine-leaved plant and some floating plants such as Riccia. A small air-driven sponge filter running gently will provide adequate filtration. It's usually recommended to drop the water level to around 6-8" and raise the temperature to 26.5 – 29 °C (80 – 84 °F). While this method certainly works, it has also been shown that if the fish are in good condition they will spawn as the mood takes them. Other parameters are not critical, provided they are within the limits suggested above. The tank should have the tightest-fitting cover you can find (some breeders use clingfilm instead, to ensure no gaps), as the fry need access to a layer of warm, humid air. Without this the development of the labyrinth organ can be impaired. Some breeders also swear by the benefits of adding dried Ketapang/Indian Almond leaves to the water of both adult and fry tanks.

The adult pair are best conditioned elsewhere before being added to the spawning tank. A diet containing plenty of live and frozen foods should soon see them in breeding condition. When the female appears to be very plump and ripe with eggs, add her to the spawning tank. Leave her there for a few days (continue to feed her) before adding the male. This is best done during the hours of darkness.

If all goes to plan the male should soon start to build his bubblenest. This begins with the construction of a raft of bubbles at the water surface. Small pieces of plant material are then used to strengthen the structure, a quite amazing behavioural sequence to observe. During this process the male will attack the female if he spots her loitering in the area, one reason why the addition of plants is essential to success. Once the nest is complete you should see a change in behaviour between the fish. The male ceases to be aggressive towards his potential mate. The female begins to play the dominant role, manouevering the male underneath the nest by nudging him with her snout and even caressing his ventral area with her "feelers".

Spawning occurs underneath the nest in the typical anabantoid "embrace", with the male wrapping himself around the female as eggs and sperm are released simultaneously. At the point of climax, the male will go very limp. The pair then come apart and the female drifts, drained of energy, to the bottom of the tank. The eggs are buoyant and as they are released float upwards and come to rest within the nest. Any that fail to do so are gathered up in the mouth of the male and placed there manually. This sequence may be repeated several times, with some resting time between each, until the female is spent of eggs. Once spawning has ended, the male takes responsibility for guarding and tending the brood. He becomes completely intolerant of his mate and she should be removed for her own safety at this point.

Hatching time is dependant on temperature, but usually occurs within 36 hours, and is signified by the nest breaking apart. Observation thorugh a magnifying glass should reveal hundreds of tiny fry. Most males are ok to leave in with the fry for the first couple of days, until they have used up their yolk sacs. It is really a matter of personal choice if you choose to leave the male with the fry until they become free swimming or remove him immediately post-hatching. The young gouramis are absoloutely minute and require infusoria-type food for the first week or so, until they're large enough to accept microworm or Artemia nauplii. You will need at least a couple of rearing tanks set up and running, in order to separate the larger and smaller fry as they grow. The fish grow at different rates and problems with bullying are common unless this kind of system is used. Individual broods can number up to 700 eggs.

Lowering the water level to 6 to 8 inches (15–20 cm) and raising the water temperature to 28 °C (82 °F) will trigger spawning. Vegetation is essential, as male gouramis construct bubble nests out of plant materials, which they then bind together with bubbles. Nests are very elaborate and sturdy, reaching several inches across (roughly 7–15 cm) and an inch (about 2.5 cm) deep. Limnophila aquatica, Riccia fluitans, Ceratopteris thalictroides, and Vesicularia dubyana are good plant choices for the breeding tank. Peat fiber can also be offered as a building material.

Once the nest has been built, the male begins courting the female, usually in the afternoon or evening. He signals his intentions by swimming around the female with flared fins, attempting to draw her to the nest where he continues his courting display. If the female accepts the male, she begins swimming in circles with the male beneath the bubble nest. When she is ready to spawn, she touches the male on either the back or the tail with her mouth.

Upon this signal the male embraces the female, turning her first on her side and finally on her back. At this point, the female releases approximately five dozen (about 60) clear eggs, which are immediately fertilized by the male. Most of the eggs float up into the bubble nest. Eggs that stray are collected by the male and placed in the nest. Once all the eggs are secured in the nest, the pair spawn again.

If more than one female is present in the breeding tank, the male may spawn with all of them. The spawning sessions continue for two to four hours and produce between 300 and 800 eggs. Upon completion, the male places a fine layer of bubbles beneath the eggs, ensuring that they remain in the bubble nest. At this point, the female(s) should be removed from the tank to reduce stress on the male.

The male then takes sole responsibility for the eggs, aggressively defending the nest and surrounding territory. In 12 to 24 hours the fry hatch and continue developing within the protection of the bubble nest. After three days they are sufficiently developed to be free-swimming.

Remove the male from the tank once the fry have left the bubble nest, or he may consume the young. Feed the fry on micro-foods such as infusoria, rotifers, or commercial fry food for the first week. After a week, they can be fed freshly hatched brine shrimp and finely ground flake foods.

Dwarf gouramis are known for bubble nesting and parental care, and under optimal conditions can be bred easily even in a confined space.

Maturity: depending on temperature, they become sexually mature in 4–12 months at about 4 cm in length. In Singapore they breed all year round and fry can mature in as little as four months, whereas in northern India it takes 8 to 12 months.

Mating:

  • Female pheromones can elicit nest-building in males.
  • The male builds a bubble nest, then courts the female by swimming around her with flared fins and touching her ventral side with his mouth.
  • Once the female responds, the male focuses on finishing the nest; the pair is ready to spawn when it is complete.
  • The female lays eggs (around five dozen clear eggs) and the male quickly fertilises them.
  • After each mating the male collects the eggs in his mouth for a few seconds and adds saliva to make them sticky, then encases them in air bubbles in the nest.
  • Spawning can continue for 2 to 4 hours, with matings several times at intervals of 30 seconds to one minute.
  • The male then guards the eggs and hatchlings and keeps the female and other fish away from the nest.

Nest: the male builds a floating bubble nest, incorporating plant bits, twigs and other debris. Build time depends on temperature: 24 hours at 28°C, 32 hours at 25°C and 72 hours at 22°C. Most eggs float up into the nest and the male collects strays.

Fecundity: absolute fecundity ranges from 1000 to 1350; females produce on average 300 to 800 eggs. Fertilisation rate is around 60%.

Eggs: spherical, 0.6–0.7 mm in diameter, golden and optically transparent. They are lighter than water and rise to the bubble nest.

Incubation: depends on temperature; around 24 hours at 23–26°C. Embryonic development passes through zygote, cleavage, blastula, gastrula, segmentation, pharyngula and hatching stages.

Fry: after hatching, fry stay attached to the bubble nest for about 2–3 days absorbing their yolk sacs; they are about 1.7–2.0 mm long and transparent. Once the yolk sac is absorbed they become dark, comma-shaped and free-swimming. The male should be removed to prevent him from eating the young. In one month fry may reach 1 cm in length and around 4 cm after 12 months.

Spawning stimulation:

  • A large tank is not needed; 4–12 litres is enough.
  • Beware of surface agitation, as some filters can disturb the bubble nest.
  • Lower the water level to around 15–20 cm.
  • Raise the temperature to 26–29°C.
  • Enrich the diet with protein-rich live food.
  • When the female's abdomen becomes visibly rounded and swollen, she is full of eggs; move her and the male to a breeding tank, doing so in the dark to minimise stress.

The Dwarf Gourami is one of the most ubiquitous freshwater species in the aquarium hobby, and is unarguably a beautiful fish. Several colour forms have been line-bred for the trade and have also proved popular. These include "Sunset" (also sold as "Red" or "Robin") and "Neon" varieties, although it's highly debatable whether these come close to matching the brilliance of the natural form.

Unfortunately the general quality of dwarf gouramis available to fishkeepers has diminished dramatically in recent years. Some shops have actually ceased to stock the species as they are unable to obtain disease-free stock from Far Eastern (primarily Singaporean) breeders and have experienced high losses. It's thought that mass-breeding for the hobby may have resulted in a widespread epidemic of a disease known as Dwarf gourami iridovirus (DGIV). This Megalocytivirus species appears to be very infectious and thus far has proved untreatable. A study conducted in Australia in 2006 revealed that as many as 22% of dwarf gouramis coming out of Singapore were carrying the disease. The apparent susceptibility of dwarf gouramis to illness was previously blamed on bacterial infections such as fish TB and Nocardia-type afflictions, but it now appears that DGIV may play a very significant role. Worryingly, it has recently been shown that DGIV can be transmitted to other species sharing the same water as an infected gourami.

It goes without saying that these fish should be observed very carefully before buying. Avoid tanks that contains lethargic-looking or darkened specimens. Ask about the origins of them, and if there have been any losses in the shop. Finding a local breeder is an option well worth considering.

Like others in the suborder Anabantoidei, the species possesses an accessory breathing organ known as the labyrinth organ. So-called due to its maze-like structure, this organ allows the fish to breathe atmospheric air to a certain extent. It is formed by a modification of the first gill arch, and consists of many highly vascularised, folded flaps of skin. The structure of the organ varies in complexity between species, tending to be more well-developed in those inhabiting particularly oxygen-deprived conditions.

The name "dwarf" fits this fish well, as it is one of the smallest of the gouramis. Males are slightly larger than females and have a bright orange-red body with turquoise-blue, vertical stripes that extend into the fins. Females remain a duller, silvery blue-gray color and never achieve the male's brilliant colors.

Several color variants have been developed by selective breeding at fish farms, including solid light blue (powder blue), neon, rainbow, and red/blushing. Powder blues are predominately blue with only a little red showing on the body. Neons display a brighter blue pattern than the standard variety. Rainbows have especially brilliant orange-red bodies with blue stripes, in addition to a green-gold metallic sheen. Reds (flame gouramis) are almost solid red throughout the body with solid blue dorsal fins.

Trichogaster lalius is generally compatible with aquarium plants and does not eat healthy plants. However, males are enthusiastic nest builders and may inadvertently damage delicate plants or uproot small ground-covering plants to incorporate fragments into their nests.

Etymology: the genus name Trichogaster comes from the Greek “trichos” and “gaster”, meaning “hair” and “belly”, referring to the hair-like pelvic appendages. The species name “lalius” is said to derive from a Latin word meaning “small” or “dwarf”, referring to its small size relative to other Trichogaster.
